pass_a_gloss: [...] not having known the Master of all, would they not even have cried at all to him? But just as the blood of Abel is said to have cried to God, and not, surely, wholly itself having its own voice, but as it were God having abhorred the very outrage of the deed, in the same way, I think, one might understand also in the case of those accustomed to worship the unclean demons. For even if they do not know the God of all, yet because they have been wronged by Satan, through the deed itself in a certain manner they have cried aloud, surely asking for help for themselves. Thus we say that the Egyptians too cried to God because of those afflicting them, that is, those who had made them under their own hand, and pressed them down as with some most bitter slavery, clearly the unclean demons. But the Lord will send them a man who will save them. And who is the man, if not clearly the Christ? That is, the only-begotten Word of God, having appeared in human form; this one has saved not Egyptians only, but indeed the whole earth too. And he saved judging; and what is the 'judging'? Instead of: bringing out a just judgment in their case. For Satan, who had wronged, and with him the unclean demons, putting under holy votes, having cast them into Tartarus with chains of gloom, he handed them over to be kept for judgment of a great day, to be punished. And those who had endured a wrong so unbearable he both saved and rescued, and showed them his own worshippers, having flashed on them the light of the truth, and having clothed them with the glories of freedom. Thus also the Saviour himself says somewhere: Now is judgment of this world. Now the ruler of this world will be cast outside. And I, if I am lifted up, will draw all to myself. You see that he has judged for the world, and has cast out Satan, who long ago tyrannized against it, and drew all to himself. For the Egyptians too have known him. And indeed, having come to know, they make sacrifices, and they vow vows, and they bring to an end the things promised. For this is what is sung through the voice of David: Vow and pay to the Lord our God. See then the newness of things. For those of old accustomed to sacrifice to the demons, those bringing the worships to Satan and dedicating thank-offerings, and indeed also fulfilling eagerly vows, that is, promises, having been enlightened in mind through Christ, and made bright by the doctrines of the truth, will run away from the ancient error, and having once come to know the generator and Lord of all, they bring to him the worship in spirit, fulfilling all-pure vows, and offering up sacrifices, no longer those through bloods and the slaughter [of irrational animals] [the section breaks off].
pass_b_english: … since they had not come to know the Master of all, would they have cried out to him at all? But just as the blood of Abel is said to have cried out to God (Genesis 4:10), not, surely, as though it had a voice of its own, but because God abhorred the very outrage of the deed, in the same way, I think, one might understand it also of those who used to worship the unclean demons. For even if they do not know the God of all, yet because they have been wronged by Satan, through the deed itself, in a manner, they have cried aloud, surely asking for help for themselves.

In this sense we say that the Egyptians too cried out to God because of those who oppressed them, that is, those who had brought them under their own hand and crushed them as with a most bitter slavery: plainly, the unclean demons. “But the Lord will send them a man who will save them” (Isaiah 19:20). And who is the man, if not, plainly, Christ, that is, the only-begotten Word of God who appeared in human form? He saved not only the Egyptians but the whole earth.

And he saved by judging. What does “by judging” mean? It means that he brought a just judgment in their case. For Satan, who had wronged them, and with him the unclean demons, he subjected to holy verdicts, cast them into Tartarus with chains of gloom, and handed them over to be kept for punishment at the judgment of the great day (compare 2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6). But those who had endured so unbearable a wrong he saved and rescued, and made them his own worshipers, flashing on them the light of truth and clothing them with the glories of freedom.

So the Savior himself says somewhere: “Now is the judgment of this world. Now the ruler of this world will be cast out. And I, if I am lifted up, will draw all to myself” (John 12:31–32). You see that he has given judgment for the world, cast out Satan, who long ago tyrannized over it, and drawn all to himself. For the Egyptians too have come to know him. And indeed, having come to know him, they offer sacrifices, they make vows, and they carry out what they promised (compare Isaiah 19:21). This is what is sung through the voice of David: “Make vows and pay them to the Lord our God” (Psalm 76:11).

See, then, the newness of things. Those who formerly used to sacrifice to demons, who brought their worship to Satan and dedicated thank offerings to him, and who eagerly fulfilled vows, that is, promises, will be enlightened in mind through Christ and made bright by the doctrines of truth. They will run from their ancient error, and having once come to know the Maker and Lord of all, they bring him worship in spirit, fulfilling most pure vows and offering sacrifices no longer through blood and the slaughter of irrational animals …

choices.english: would they have cried out to him at all?
choices.why: The opening is a question in the Greek, and the question form is kept.

choices.english: God abhorred the very outrage of the deed
choices.why: The genitive absolute makes God the one who abhors the deed.
rejected: the atrocity of the deed disturbing God
